title: Data Export and Reporting Snapshots
learningObjectives: Distinguish SQL result selection from file export operations.
Create a stable reporting snapshot from transactional data.
Use explicit columns and deterministic ordering for exports.
Record export metadata without storing credentials.
Explain why CSV formatting and file delivery are handled by client or database tooling.

understand.concept: An export is a controlled representation of selected database data delivered to another system or file. SQL prepares the rows; the application, driver or database utility usually serializes and transfers them.
understand.whyItMatters: Exports are often used for reporting, finance and integrations. Unstable ordering, changing source rows or excessive columns can make an export unreliable or expose unnecessary information.
understand.analogy: A warehouse prepares a labelled shipment list, while the carrier packages and delivers the shipment.
understand.analogyLimit: A SELECT statement does not itself create a downloadable CSV file in a browser. File creation, encoding, quoting and delivery belong to a client or database utility.

explain.narrative:
## Export workflow
Choose the exact columns and row filters, define a deterministic order, decide whether the export is a live query or a point-in-time snapshot, then serialize the result with a client or database export utility. Use an explicit schema/version for downstream consumers.

## Reporting snapshots
A snapshot table can preserve the result of a report at a chosen time. It should include a batch or snapshot identifier and a generated timestamp so later consumers can distinguish different exports.

## CSV and file handling
CSV quoting, delimiter, encoding, line endings and NULL representation are not defined by SELECT itself. The application or command-line utility handles these details. Do not put database passwords, API tokens or file-storage credentials in export metadata.

examples.title: Create a source sales table
examples.code: CREATE TABLE ops21_sales (sale_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, sold_on TEXT NOT NULL, region TEXT NOT NULL, amount INTEGER NOT NULL);
examples.explanation: Creates the source rows for a reporting export. The date is ISO-formatted text for this SQLite example; a production design should use the target engine's date/time type where appropriate.

examples.title: Insert sample sales
examples.explanation: Adds four sales records across two regions and two dates. These values provide a known total of 400.

examples.title: Create a reporting snapshot table
examples.code: CREATE TABLE ops21_export_snapshot (snapshot_id INTEGER NOT NULL, region TEXT NOT NULL, total_amount INTEGER NOT NULL, generated_at TEXT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (snapshot_id, region));
examples.explanation: Defines a composite key so each snapshot can contain one row per region. generated_at records when the report was materialized.

examples.title: Materialize one regional report snapshot
examples.code: INSERT INTO ops21_export_snapshot SELECT 1, region, SUM(amount), '2026-11-22T10:00:00Z' FROM ops21_sales GROUP BY region;
examples.explanation: Captures the current regional totals in snapshot 1: East 200 and West 200. The inserted rows remain stable even if the source sales table changes later.

examples.title: Read the snapshot in export order
examples.code: SELECT region, total_amount, generated_at FROM ops21_export_snapshot WHERE snapshot_id = 1 ORDER BY region;
examples.explanation: Returns a deterministic export dataset. A client or database utility must serialize these rows to CSV or another file format and apply the required quoting and encoding rules.

practise.guidedTask: Run the examples and compare the live sales table with the stored snapshot. Explain why a snapshot is useful when source data may change after an export is generated.
practise.independentTask: Design a monthly export snapshot with a unique batch ID, generated timestamp and one row per department. Specify the CSV encoding, NULL representation and deterministic ordering expected by the receiving system.
hints: SELECT returns rows; client tools create files.
Use explicit columns and a stable ORDER BY.
Snapshots preserve the result at a point in time.
Record snapshot ID and generated timestamp.
Never store export credentials in metadata.

questions.prompt: Does a plain SELECT statement create a CSV file?
options: No; a client or database utility serializes the result
Only when the query has GROUP BY
questions.answer: No; a client or database utility serializes the result
questions.explanation: SQL selects rows; file creation is handled by a tool or application.

options: To preserve a report result at a chosen point in time
To change the source data type
questions.answer: To preserve a report result at a chosen point in time
questions.explanation: A snapshot makes a report reproducible after source rows change.

questions.prompt: Why is ORDER BY important for an export?
options: It provides a deterministic row sequence
questions.answer: It provides a deterministic row sequence
questions.explanation: A stable order supports repeatable files and comparisons.

questions.prompt: Which CSV concern is not defined by SELECT itself?
questions.explanation: The serializer or export utility handles the file representation.

questions.prompt: What should export metadata avoid storing?
questions.explanation: Metadata should never become a store for access secrets.
